packets.key_finding: A nudge that shrinks the visibility of the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cuts minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but does not significantly reduce debt, because nudged cardholders opt for autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and some drop out of autopay entirely, raising missed payments.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts with six-month follow-up, comparing nudged vs. control cardholders' autopay enrollment and payment behavior.
packets.why_it_matters: This is direct evidence for the support team's 'vanity enrollment' worry in a genuinely consumer, self-directed financial product: a choice-architecture nudge changed nominal behavior without changing the substantive outcome (debt paid down), which is exactly the enrollment-vs-amount distinction the round-up feature decision turns on.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
nudge shrouded an option rather than setting a full opt-out default
packets.relevance_reason: Closest consumer-financial-product evidence that enrollment metrics can diverge sharply from the amount-level outcome the feature is meant to produce.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on 2020 US campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, less-experienced donors who likely did not intend a recurring commitment.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across multiple political campaign websites that added pre-checked recurring-donation boxes at different times; observational/quasi-experimental.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest real-world evidence that a pre-checked recurring-contribution default can lift nominal sign-up while simultaneously generating regret and complaints in the least-experienced users — precisely the support team's objection, quantified.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product
refund requests are a proxy for regret, not a direct complaint or withdrawal metric
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise with a large quantified estimate of both benefit and consumer detriment, plus the exact heterogeneity (inexperienced, small users) the brief asks about.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when and how default effects persist or fade downstream, identifying time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as the key moderators of long-run default effects.
packets.methodology: Conceptual review and framework synthesis of the consumer-default literature; no new primary data.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the project a structured way to predict which of our two design choices (entry, level) is likely to show a lasting vs. fading effect, and why enrolled-but-disengaged users are a documented, theorized pattern rather than an anecdote from support.
limitations: conceptual synthesis, not a quantitative meta-analysis
no numeric effect sizes to anchor design decisions
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: The review-level synthesis the brief asks for on whether and how default effects persist versus decay, in a genuinely consumer (non-employer) framing.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (especially one people refuse) lowers users' rating of the advice/wealth manager, an effect mediated by perceived honesty; question framing in the default presentation also shifts chosen allocations.
packets.methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, manipulating default presence and framing of investment defaults.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the EU-consumer-relevant reputational cost of defaults — a default that people override actively damages trust — which bears squarely on whether an opt-out round-up default will read as helpful or manipulative, and on how the preset multiplier should be framed to avoid an anchoring/dark-pattern read.
limitations: wealth-management investment-allocation context, not a round-up savings app
advisor-mediated setting differs somewhat from a purely self-service app flow
packets.relevance_reason: The only EU-context experimental evidence quantifying when a default is perceived as manipulative, and how framing of the default level shifts chosen amounts — bears directly on both the entry and level decisions.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6 percentage points from automatic enrollment and 0.3 points from default auto-escalation once job separation, unvested-balance withdrawal, and auto-escalation opt-out are accounted for; only 40% of those defaulted into auto-escalation follow through on the first scheduled increase.
packets.methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover, withdrawal-on-separation, and auto-escalation opt-out dynamics.
packets.why_it_matters: The single strongest quantified rebuttal to the 'defaults will lift enrolment, so default everyone in' argument: it shows the true steady-state effect of automatic enrollment/escalation is far smaller than headline participation-rate lifts suggest, directly undercutting the internal case for full opt-out enrollment.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-plan mechanics (vesting, job separation) don't map onto a banking app
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving amounts, which the brief explicitly asked us to test.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: At-scale field experiments at major UK banks show automatic enrollment into just-in-time text alerts reduced unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though alerts captured less than half of potential avoidable savings.
packets.methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments across major UK retail banks; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest real-world precedent for opt-out enrollment inside an existing consumer banking app: it quantifies both the size of the behavior-change benefit and its shortfall relative to full potential, which is exactly the trade-off the enrolment-default decision needs measured against.
limitations: overdraft alerts, not a savings/round-up feature
no explicit 6-12 month persistence breakdown given in the abstract
packets.relevance_reason: Directly on-point: UK retail-bank consumer product, opt-out/auto-enrollment mechanism, quantified real behavioral and monetary effects, not an employer-mediated setting.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects sustained at least 15 months, showing active choice screens can meaningfully shift default-driven behavior.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the staggered EU DMA choice-screen rollout across iOS and Android; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests whether a mandated active-choice screen (the exact 'active choice' onboarding design under consideration) produces large, persistent behavior change relative to a preset default, in an EU regulatory context comparable to ours.
limitations: browser default, not a financial savings product
no individual-level enrollment/engagement or complaint data
packets.relevance_reason: The closest empirical evidence on whether forced active choice meaningfully changes outcomes relative to defaults, under the same EU regulatory regime the product will operate in.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with default-option and positive-narrative nudges producing the largest backfire, and effects varying by income, education, gender, and financial motivation.
packets.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions; N=220.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving: here the default option nudge backfires and lowers willingness to contribute, with heterogeneity by demographic group that mirrors the brief's distributional concern.
limitations: hypothetical/survey-based willingness rather than real enrollment behavior
small sample (N=220) and a different cultural/regulatory context (China, not EU)
pension savings context rather than liquid round-up savings
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in this batch that a default can actively reduce rather than raise contribution intentions, satisfying the brief's explicit request for a contradicting paper.
packets.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
packets.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
packets.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

packets.key_finding: This NBER handbook chapter synthesises household finance evidence on savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, and surveys interventions including choice architecture, product design, and default effects used by firms and governments to shape financial behaviour.
packets.methodology: Narrative literature review/handbook chapter (Beshears, Choi, Laibson, Madrian).
packets.why_it_matters: Provides the broad review-level synthesis of choice-architecture effect sizes and mechanisms across household finance that the brief explicitly asks for, giving a check on whether single-study estimates generalise before the round-up feature is built.
limitations: narrative overview, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
covers many domains at a high level rather than round-up savings specifically
abstract-only detail on which parts concern consumer defaults versus employer plans
packets.relevance_reason: The review/synthesis needed in the evidence portfolio to check single-study default effect estimates against the broader household-finance literature.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, each $1 of tax-subsidy expenditure raised total saving by only 1 cent because 85% of people are 'passive savers' unmoved by subsidies but heavily influenced by automatic contributions, while the 15% who are 'active' mainly shift assets across accounts rather than saving more.
packets.methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis (Denmark, ~41 million observations) exploiting variation between active-choice subsidy policies and automatic/passive contribution policies.
packets.why_it_matters: The strongest available evidence that a default changes real accumulated wealth for the majority who are passive, not merely who is nominally enrolled — directly answers the brief's question of whether defaults change the amount saved versus just enrolment counts, and shows the effect is concentrated among the financially less sophisticated, informing who is helped.
limitations: government retirement/tax-advantaged accounts in Denmark, not a self-directed liquid consumer app
the employer/state-as-intermediary trust mechanism the brief flags as non-transferable may partly drive the passive-saver result
no data on withdrawal or disengagement of passive savers
packets.relevance_reason: Uniquely detailed evidence distinguishing nominal enrolment from real savings impact across active/passive saver types, the closest existing answer to the brief's central 'vanity metric' question.
packets.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
packets.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

alternates.key_finding: Across three large firms, automatic enrollment pushed 401(k) participation above 85%, but about 80% initially accepted both the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default conservative fund, and half of participants were still on the default rate and fund after three years.
alternates.methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large US firms comparing pre/post automatic-enrollment cohorts.
alternates.why_it_matters: The most quantitatively detailed evidence available on whether a preset level anchors people at that level and whether this persists over years rather than fading — directly bears on whether shipping a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor most users there long after signup.
limitations: employer 401(k) context, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
measures retirement contribution/fund choice anchoring, not a round-up multiplier
no explicit engagement/complaint or withdrawal-rate data
alternates.relevance_reason: Strongest and most detailed evidence on default-level anchoring and its multi-year persistence, the closest analogue to the preset-multiplier decision despite the employer setting.
alternates.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
alternates.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

alternates.key_finding: A reminder nudge in a Brazilian consumer financial app reduced credit-card late fees by 14% but increased overdraft fees by 9%, with a net 5% fee increase for users with a history of overdraft use while other users saved 15%.
alternates.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform (Brazil), comparing fee outcomes between nudged and control users, with subgroup analysis by overdraft history.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's concern that a well-intentioned intervention can help most users while harming a vulnerable subgroup — the exact distributional risk the team must check before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level presets
outcome is fee incidence, not savings enrolment or amount saved
Brazilian credit-card context differs from EU round-up savings regulatory setting
alternates.relevance_reason: Strongest available RCT evidence that a nudge can produce net harm for an identifiable subgroup even while helping the average user, bearing directly on the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk question (C5).
alternates.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
alternates.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision, no default) and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option can motivate behaviour change as a complement or alternative to automatic enrollment when opt-out defaults are infeasible or unethical.
alternates.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against no-intervention/default baselines, building on Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick's active-choice framework.
alternates.why_it_matters: This is the primary source for the 'active choice' design option itself, directly informing whether forcing a yes/no answer at onboarding can capture most of the enrolment benefit of opt-out without its ethical/manipulation downsides — the exact trade-off decision 1 is weighing.
limitations: field experiments largely in medication-adherence contexts rather than financial products
no long-term (6-12 month) persistence or withdrawal data reported
abstract does not give quantitative effect sizes for the enhanced active choice condition
alternates.relevance_reason: The originating method/design precedent for active choice as an alternative to opt-out defaults, the mechanism central to the entry-design decision (C6).
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, are attenuated by 36 months; average savings increases are modest at the longer horizon, though inequality in savings is significantly reduced, and a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
alternates.methodology: Empirical analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
alternates.why_it_matters: This is the closest available quantified answer to the brief's central persistence question — does the default effect on enrolment survive past sign-up — showing attenuation over time even in the closest available analogous literature, which should temper expectations for the round-up feature's 6-12 month enrolment numbers.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a self-directed consumer app
life-cycle model calibrated to retirement savings, not small liquid round-ups
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides the most directly quantified estimate of default-effect attenuation over medium-run horizons, the closest prior work on the persistence question the brief asks about.
alternates.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
alternates.abstract: Using data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, I document the impact of auto-enrollment (AE) on retirement savings at different horizons. I replicate the impact of AE on participation and contributions in the short run (at 12 months), but I show that these gains are attenuated over the medium run (at 36 months). At this longer horizon, the average savings increases are modest, though AE significantly lowers inequality in savings. To assess AE’s lifetime impact, I estimate a life cycle consumption-savings model that can fit the observed patterns with a switching cost of approximately $250, smaller than previous estimates. (JEL D15, G51, J26, J32)

alternates.key_finding: In an opt-in short-term (withdrawable-anytime) savings program at five UK firms, at most 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account, but among those who did, 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received an automatic contribution 12 months later.
alternates.methodology: Field study of program rollout and account activity at five UK employers, tracking activation and 12-month account balances/contributions.
alternates.why_it_matters: The closest available real-world analog to the round-up feature itself — a liquid, withdrawable, opt-in savings product — showing the exact trade-off the brief asks about: opt-in produces very low take-up but strong sustained engagement among those who join, directly informing the entry-mode decision.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction channel, not a standalone banking app
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice arms in the same study
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly matches the product type (liquid, withdrawable, opt-in short-term savings) and quantifies the low-uptake/high-persistence trade-off central to the entry decision.
alternates.title: Employer-Based Short-Term Savings Accounts
alternates.abstract: We study the introduction of a choice architecture design intended to increase short-term savings among employees at five U.K. firms. Employees were offered the opportunity to opt into a payroll deduction program that auto-deposits funds from each paycheck into a short-term savings account from which withdrawals are possible at any time. We find that employees who opted into the program kept using it. Among employees whose accounts were created early enough to be observed over the first 12 months after their account activation and who did not separate from employment during this period, 96% still had a balance greater than 1 and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution in month 12. However, product take-up was very low: no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account. Opt-in access to short-term savings programs does not elicit widespread participation.
